profiles.meeting_scenario: A mid-sized Japanese teaching hospital has piloted an internal self-reflection reporting process for internists after a journal club discussed a national survey on memorable diagnostic error cases. After six weeks, only seven cases have been submitted, and most are sparse, weekday cases despite repeated anecdotal mention of missed or delayed diagnoses in outpatient clinic and the emergency department. The meeting is a troubleshooting session between the physician leading diagnostic learning and the patient safety manager overseeing the reporting workflow. Their agenda is to figure out why clinicians are not submitting usable cases, identify the most likely root causes in the current process, and agree on a practical fix before the next quarterly diagnostic safety conference.

members.name: Dr. Aki Tanabe
members.role: Director of General Internal Medicine Quality Improvement
members.expertise: Diagnostic reasoning, ambulatory internal medicine, case-based physician education
members.background: A senior internist who runs monthly diagnostic case conferences and previously worked in both outpatient clinic and emergency department observation units.
members.private_state: Wants psychologically safe, educational case collection that surfaces near-misses and wrong initial impressions before they disappear from memory; worries that clinicians are avoiding the tool because it feels like punitive incident reporting rather than reflective learning.
hidden_assumptions: A 'diagnostic error case' includes wrong initial working diagnoses that were corrected later the same day if the reasoning failure is instructive.
When colleagues mention a 'consultation barrier,' they usually mean not being able to informally reach a supervisor or specialist in real time during clinic or overnight care.
A 'complete case' means the narrative contains the timeline, initial differential, key missed clue, and what triggered diagnostic revision.
To 'streamline intake' can include a brief verbal debrief captured later by staff, as long as the physician records the clinical story while it is still vivid.

members.name: Naomi Sato
members.expertise: Incident reporting systems, clinical risk review, workflow design, nursing operations
members.background: A former emergency department nurse who now manages the hospital's safety reporting platform, committee review packets, and de-identification procedures.
members.private_state: Wants a defensible, auditable submission process that can go through safety review without privacy or legal problems; worries that broadening the definition or moving off-platform will create unusable reports and extra follow-up work.
hidden_assumptions: A 'diagnostic error case' should generally involve a documented wrong, missed, or delayed diagnosis with meaningful patient impact or a clear downstream consequence.
A 'consultation barrier' commonly refers to the inability to get formal review or interdepartmental response through normal channels on weekends or after hours.
A 'complete case' means all required structured fields are filled, the attending and service are identified, and patient details are sufficiently de-identified for committee handling.
To 'streamline intake' means simplifying the existing secure web form and submission steps, not replacing it with interviews or side-channel note capture.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a diagnostic error case
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to increasing 'diagnostic error case' submissions
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Tanabe means any memorable case with a flawed initial diagnostic frame, including near-misses and same-day corrections that still reveal reasoning problems.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Sato means cases that meet a more formal safety-event threshold, usually involving documented delay, miss, or harm substantial enough for review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in quality improvement and use the same institutional language, so 'diagnostic error case' sounds settled; the divergence only affects which cases they imagine clinicians should submit, not the surface wording of the meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'consultation barrier' weekend cases refer to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'weekend consultation barriers' as a reason cases are underreported
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Tanabe is thinking of front-line clinical situations where a physician could not quickly reach a supervisor or specialty colleague for diagnostic input during clinic closing hours or overnight coverage.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Sato is thinking of the reporting and review pathway, where safety submissions and cross-department responses stall over weekends until risk-management staff return on Monday.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same phrase plausibly describes both the clinical and administrative bottleneck, and in a diagnostic-safety discussion neither interpretation sounds out of place enough to trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need more 'complete cases'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Tanabe means cases with enough clinical narrative to reconstruct reasoning: symptom evolution, initial differential, missed data, and pivot point.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Sato means cases with every required field entered and appropriately de-identified so they can move through committee review without rework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In healthcare quality work, 'complete' naturally implies both usable clinical detail and administratively finished documentation, so each hears confirmation of their own standard.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the hospital should 'streamline intake' or 'shorten the form'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dr. Tanabe assumes this could mean a quick initial story capture followed by a short verbal debrief or later staff-assisted transcription.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Sato assumes this means reducing mandatory fields inside the current secure web form while keeping the same submission channel and documentation structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the surface level, both are endorsing efficiency rather than debating the workflow itself, so the method remains implicit and each person imagines the familiar version used in their own work.

turns.inner_thought: Seven submissions in six weeks is far below what people are actually talking about in conference hallways. I keep hearing memorable wrong first impressions from clinic and ED observation, especially cases that were corrected later the same day, but those are exactly the ones disappearing before anyone writes them down. If the process feels like incident reporting, people will avoid it because they do not want to implicate themselves over an instructive near-miss.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to look at this early because the reflective reporting pilot is not giving us what we hoped for. We have only seven submissions from medicine so far, and that does not match what people are informally discussing after clinic and in the ED. There are clearly more memorable diagnostic error cases out there than what is reaching the system.

turns.inner_thought: The analytics are pretty clear: physicians click in, then abandon the form. The drop-off is worst for cases noticed on weekends or after hours, which makes sense because the normal safety review chain and cross-service follow-up do not really move until Monday. They may not want to start something that they know will sit in the queue and then require formal review standards.
turns.utterance: I pulled the workflow data this morning. The biggest drop-off is after physicians open the form rather than before. There is also a noticeable pattern around weekend consultation barriers and after-hours submissions, so it does not look like simple lack of awareness.

turns.inner_thought: That fits exactly with the clinical reality I am worried about. The memorable cases often happen when someone cannot quickly grab a supervisor or specialist late in clinic or overnight, and then the initial diagnosis gets revised later once fresh eyes or new data come in. Those are gold for teaching diagnostic reasoning, even when the correction happens fast and the patient does okay.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. A lot of the memorable diagnostic error cases come up when people hit weekend consultation barriers late in clinic or overnight, especially the ones where the diagnosis is later corrected. Those are often the cases people talk about most, but they still never seem to get entered.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and once they see that the case has to fit the safety-event definition and go through the standard route, they back out. If it does not clearly meet the documented threshold for wrong, missed, or delayed diagnosis with some consequence, they may decide it is not worth the trouble, especially if the review will not even move until after the weekend staffing gap resolves.
turns.utterance: What I am hearing from a few people is similar. They start, then stop once they realize the case has to fit the diagnostic error fields and move through the usual review pathway after the weekend. I think that is a bigger deterrent than we expected.

turns.inner_thought: For the conference, I do not need a polished incident packet. I need enough clinical story to reconstruct the reasoning arc: when the symptoms evolved, what the first frame was, what clue was missed, and what finally made the team rethink it. If I can get that while the case is still vivid, we can turn it into educational material later.
turns.utterance: From my side, what would help most is getting more complete cases. If we have the timeline, the first diagnostic impression, and what clue changed the team's thinking, we can do something useful with it at conference. Right now many of the submissions are too thin to learn from.

turns.inner_thought: I agree on complete cases, but in practice that means the required fields are all there, the responsible attending and service are named, and the details are cleaned enough that committee packets do not create privacy or legal problems. My team loses time chasing basic omissions, and that follow-up is exactly what makes this unsustainable if volume increases.
turns.utterance: I agree, we need more complete cases. The problem for us is that incomplete entries are hard to use operationally, because once required pieces are missing we have to go back and chase people afterward. That creates rework for my team and slows everything down.

turns.inner_thought: The solution seems straightforward: capture the story immediately, even in a very brief way, while the reasoning is still fresh after a shift. The rest can be filled in later or supported by staff. If we insist that the physician finish a full report in one sitting, we will keep losing the most educational near-misses.
turns.utterance: Then I think we should streamline intake. If physicians can capture the story quickly right after a shift and deal with the rest once the case is calmer, we are much more likely to get those submissions before the details fade.

turns.inner_thought: I can work with that, as long as it stays inside the secure reporting platform. We can shorten the current web form, trim a few fields, and probably get it under five minutes without breaking the audit trail or de-identification steps. I do not want parallel interviews or side notes floating around outside the system.
turns.utterance: Yes, streamlining intake is reasonable. My first thought is that we shorten the form inside the current web workflow so it takes under five minutes but still keeps the secure submission process intact. That would lower the threshold without creating a separate pathway.

turns.inner_thought: So the core issue is probably that clinicians encounter real bedside consultation problems and then face a form that feels like formal incident review rather than reflective learning. If we make first capture lighter, we might finally get the cases people mention in passing but never write down.
turns.utterance: I think that is probably the heart of it. Clinicians run into real weekend consultation barriers, and then the diagnostic error form feels heavier than reflective case capture. That combination is enough to stop people, even when the case itself is highly worth discussing.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I will revise the instructions to make the threshold and steps feel clearer, and I will pare down the web form while preserving the review requirements. If we can get more complete cases through the existing secure channel before next quarter, the committee will have something defensible to review and maybe clinicians will stop abandoning the page.
turns.utterance: That sounds like a practical next step. I will revise the instructions and shorten the form before next quarter, and we can see whether that improves the number of complete case submissions coming in for review. If the uptake changes, we will know we were blocking people at intake.
